newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Ex-dictator returns to Nicaraguan spotlight.
newsitem.headline: Ex-dictator returns to Nicaraguan spotlight.

text.p: The legacy of former dictator Anastasio Somoza returned to centre stage in Nicaragua on Friday as political groups grappled over what to do with his confiscated properties.
Somoza's family ruled Nicaragua with an iron fist for 43 years, accumulating vast properties and businesses while in power, before being toppled by the 1979 Sandinista revolution.

The left-wing revolutionary government confiscated the dictator's properties, along with tens of thousands of other privately owned farms, houses and businesses, creating conflicts between the former and current occupants that still have not been resolved.

Late on Thursday, delegations from Nicaragua's new right-wing government and the Sandinistas met in the third round of negotiations to resolve the property disputes, which have scared investment away from Nicaragua for years.

Congressman Bayardo Arce, the head of the Sandinista delegation, told reporters on Friday the delegations agreed to form a commission to analyse each side's proposals and the legality of confiscations dating back to the Somoza era.
But once again the delegations butted heads over the possibility of returning properties confiscated from Somoza to his family members, most of whom live in the United States.

Nicaraguan President Arnoldo Aleman has said his government does not want to return Somoza's former properties to his family, but family members can take their case to Nicaragua's courts, and if the courts rule in their favour the government will support the decision.
Arce said the return of properties to the Somozas was unacceptable since most of these properties were acquired illegitimately by Somoza.
"There should be an investigation into the ill-gotten possessions of the Somozas," he said.
Other Sandinista groups reacted more heatedly to the possibility of the Somozas getting their land back or being compensated financially.

"Aleman's invitation to the Somozas to return and claim their properties is a dangerous provocation. It seems they want a confrontation," Gloria Martinez Largaespada, head of the Nicaraguan Association of Mother Heroes and Martyrs, said in the Sandinista-owned newspaper Barricada on Friday.

Arce said among the properties being reclaimed by the Somozas were about 250,000 hectares (618,000 acres) of land, including the land on which Managua's Metropolitan Cathedral was built, and the Spanish-owned beach resort of Montelimar.

Anastasio Somoza seized power in Nicaragua in a coup in 1937 and ruled, with one brief interruption, until his assassination in 1956. He was succeeded by his older son, who ruled until 1963. His second son, Anastasio Somoza Debayle, ruled from 1967-1972 and again from 1974 until the Sandanista revolution in 1979. He fled to Paraguay, where he was assassinated.
